analysis.investment_thesis: Cohance (formerly Suven Pharma) presents a deteriorating earnings picture — net profit has fallen from INR 454 Cr (FY22) to INR 265 Cr (FY25), a 42% decline — yet the market still values it at 49.7x trailing earnings and an EV/EBITDA of 94.7x. This combination of contracting fundamentals and speculative pricing is precisely what the intelligent investor must avoid.
key_strengths: Operating cash flow has been positive every year (INR 288–407 Cr range), confirming earnings are real and not accounting constructs
Debt/equity of 0.11 is modest, and the company carries adequate cash reserves
High gross margin of 71.5% suggests genuine value-added manufacturing rather than pass-through chemistry
key_risks: Earnings have declined for three consecutive years (FY23–FY25): operating income contracted from INR 574 Cr to INR 375 Cr — the business is shrinking in real terms
Total assets nearly tripled from INR 2,254 Cr to INR 5,568 Cr in FY25 alone, with borrowings jumping from INR 65 Cr to INR 451 Cr — a major acquisition whose economics are unproven
Operating margin of only 8.89% is dangerously thin for a specialty pharma CDMO; any pricing pressure or customer loss destroys profitability
red_flags: Graham Number ≈ INR 133 (EPS ~INR 7.9, BVPS ~INR 99); current price of INR 391 is 2.9x that figure
EV/EBITDA of 94.7x is not a valuation — it is speculation; I have never paid such a multiple in my career
Net profit declining three years running while the P/E expands is the definition of a value trap in reverse — a growth story with no growth
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The fundamental problem with Cohance is that the story has moved in exactly the wrong direction. Revenue peaked at INR 1,340 Cr in FY23 and remains below that level; EBITDA has contracted from INR 639 Cr to INR 419 Cr; net profit has fallen from INR 454 Cr to INR 265 Cr. A business I would insist on buying only at a significant discount to proven earning power cannot be bought here at any reasonable price — the trailing multiple already discounts a recovery that may not materialise.

The sudden balance-sheet expansion in FY25 (total assets from INR 2,254 Cr to INR 5,568 Cr) suggests a substantial acquisition was completed, likely using a combination of equity and new borrowings (debt rose from INR 65 Cr to INR 279 Cr in total debt terms). The returns on this acquired capital are completely unknown. When a business I already find overpriced doubles its asset base through an acquisition of uncertain quality, my only response is to step aside entirely.
